item.title: Pan-African School Games 2026: Celebrating Young Talent, School Pride and New Opportunities
item.description: The Pan-African School Games 2026 brought together young athletes from schools across Lagos for three days of swimming, athletics and football, celebrating sporting talent, school pride and the opportunities that organized competition can create for children and young people. Held at James Hope College, Lekki, from 16 to 18 October, the second edition of the Games featured the U-11, U-13 and U-15 categories. Students competed for individual honours and school points while gaining valuable experience in a structured, multi-sport environment. The competition also welcomed sporting stakeholders and scouts, reinforcing the wider ambition of the Pan-African School Games: to give young athletes a platform where their abilities can be demonstrated, recognized and developed. Building on the Inaugural Games The second edition of the Pan-African School Games built on the foundation established by the inaugural Games in 2025, continuing the vision of creating meaningful sporting opportunities for young athletes. The 2026 edition welcomed schools and student-athletes for three days of swimming, athletics and football, providing a platform for competition, talent development and school pride. Beyond the sporting results, the Games continued to advance a broader ambition: to connect schools, athletes, sporting stakeholders and educational institutions while creating opportunities for young people to develop their abilities and explore future pathways through sport. Day One: Swimming Opens the Games Swimming opened the competition, bringing young swimmers together for races across the U-11, U-13 and U-15 categories. The opening day set the pace for the Games as athletes took to the pool to test their abilities, pursue strong performances and earn points for their schools. The races highlighted the preparation, discipline and technique required to compete, while providing young swimmers with valuable experience in a formal sporting environment. For many of the students, the opportunity to compete alongside athletes from other schools added to the significance of the experience. Each race contributed to the overall competition, with schools beginning their campaigns for medals and category honours. Organized by Afreximbank in collaboration with the African Union and the AfCFTA Secretariat, Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX WKND) is Africa’s premier event celebrating the continent’s creative and cultural industries. Under the overarching theme “One People, United in Culture, Creating for the World: From FESTAC ’77 to CANEX ’27,” this year’s gathering will connect thousands of creative entrepreneurs, investors, policymakers, and cultural icons from across Global Africa and the diaspora. Spotlighting Francophone Luxury & Made-in-Africa Fashion As part of this landmark event, Afrique Femme is hosting a dedicated Exhibition Pavilion designed to bridge Francophone and Anglophone creative ecosystems. The pavilion will feature curated showcases, pop-ups, and private sales from leading West and Central African designers. Attendees will experience exclusive collections from celebrated brands including Makeda by AYA Konan ,, KUMI , KWELAKU , and Galipette Atelier , highlighting the richness, craftsmanship, and global potential of Francophone fashion. The African Woman 2.0 VIP Networking Brunch A core highlight of the week will take place on Saturday, November 7, 2026 , with the African Woman 2.0 VIP Networking Brunch . Bringing together 200 to 250 influential women leaders, policymakers, innovators, and international dignitaries, the high-level gathering will feature keynote addresses, strategic panels, and structured B2B networking aimed at fostering female leadership and economic empowerment across the continent. “We are thrilled to bring the African Woman 2.0 platform to Lagos alongside CANEX WKND 2026,” said Aïssata Sidibé N’DIA , Managing Director of RED Côte d’Ivoire / Afrique Femme. “This partnership offers an extraordinary opportunity to celebrate the ingenuity of African creative entrepreneurs, showcase Francophone fashion excellence on a global stage, and build lasting cross-border trade and investment synergies across Africa.” Event & Registration Details Dates: November 5–8, 2026 Venue: Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture & Creative Arts (National Theatre), Lagos, Nigeria Registration: Delegate attendance at CANEX WKND 2026 is 100% free , but pre-registration is mandatory. item.title: African Philanthropy Leaders Call for Bolder, Locally Led Giving at the 2026 APF Conference in Cape Town
item.description: CAPE TOWN, South Africa: African Philanthropy Forum (APF) closed its 2026 Conference in Cape Town on 27 October with a message that ran through nearly every session: Africa’s challenges are connected, so African giving has to be connected too. Held from 25 to 27 October under the theme Bridge the Divide; Reimagine the Future , the conference brought together philanthropists, funders, business leaders, creatives, and technologists to ask how African capital can be mobilized, how partnerships can be strengthened, and how African-led solutions can be backed with more trust and flexibility. Centered on Africa, the program also looked outward, drawing on solutions from across the Global South and asking how African philanthropy can bridge the divide. The conference opened on Sunday evening with a reception at Cape Point Vineyards, where Executive Director Mosun Layode welcomed delegates, members and acknowledged APF Board members, including Chair Gbenga Oyebode , Wale Adeosun , and Nyimpini Mabunda . Former Board Member Phuthi Mahanyele-Dabengwa urged guests to look past the continent’s challenges and toward its potential and to use the days ahead to turn conversations into partnerships. It was an evening of connection before two days of ideas at the Norval Foundation. Reimagining the Future Monday, 26 October, began with a call to build bridges across regions, languages, and funding silos. Mosun Layode and Gbenga Oyebode officially opened and welcomed all delegates to the conference. Dr. Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka , former Vice President of South Africa, spoke of education as a sacred right of every African child and of bringing young people into decision-making. In the first keynote, Gary Lubner, Founder of the This Day Foundation, described giving away 95 percent of his wealth during his lifetime and said it was easier and more joyful than holding it for heirs. Old money thinking, he argued, is a major barrier to giving, and generosity includes time and effort as well as cash. The numbers framed the challenge. Delegates heard that Africa needs about $1.3 trillion in financing each year, while philanthropy contributes $5 billion to $6 billion. The task is to use that small pool to unlock far larger sources, such as pension funds and fixed-income assets, so money reaches businesses that create jobs. In an afternoon keynote moderated by Marlene Ogawa of Synergos, Phuthi Mahanyele-Dabengwa , South Africa CEO of Naspers, and Gareth Ackerman, Non-Executive Director at Pick n Pay, kept things practical: back women entrepreneurs without taking equity, start with your own family and community, use local distributors, and make it easier to travel between African countries. One retraining program they discussed moved 7,200 of 8,000 university graduates into tech jobs. The difference between charity and philanthropy, they said, is helping people help themselves. The day also asked hard questions about who belongs. A panel on migration, moderated by Dr Ndidi Okonkw

item.title: AI & Equity: The Big Conversations at Goalkeepers Dakar 2026
item.description: The Goalkeepers 2026 Event in Dakar brought together innovators, global leaders and experts on how AI can be further leveraged by Africans for an equitable future On October 29, 2026, Africans gathered in Dakar, Senegal, to discuss the continent’s relationship with the world’s fastest-growing technology: artificial intelligence (AI). This event was part of the Goalkeepers 2026 series and was themed “Make This Matter: Equitable AI and the Future of African Youth .” It brought together professionals and innovators who focused on how Africa can adopt AI to fill gaps and ensure equitable access across various sectors . Africans are leveraging AI for business, education and more, but as AI continues to develop and expand rapidly, it is crucial for us to use it on a bigger scale, ensuring collective development and an equitable future for all. This makes the Goalkeepers 2026 event in Dakar particularly significant. Nigerian influencer, Saskay, at Goalkeepers Dakar 2026 The event included several activities, including performances from the legendary Youssou N’Dour , a Qui veut changer le monden session where people pitched their ideas, conversations about AI and equity and more. Here are some of the major talking points at the event: AI and Existing Solutions The event was graciously hosted in English and French by Fatou Jupiter Toure , who opened by sharing a powerful African message: “It is not about what you can do. It is about what we can do for each other.” Despite the diverse cultures and beliefs that exist on the continent, Africans have remained held by the belief of “I am because you are.” This is why, despite AI’s fast growth, Africans are coming together to examine how much it concerns them, how it can be properly leveraged and what dangers and challenges lie ahead. Fatou Jupiter Toure hosting the Goalkeepers 2026 event in Dakar Nevertheless, Africans have done a great deal of work with AI. Innovators have used AI tools to provide solutions in their local communities. Vyonne Njeri shared how she got into healthcare and how AI has been greatly helping in the community she serves. In the Goalkeepers 2026 Report , Vyonne said she got into healthcare during a visit to see her uncle, a priest in a small, East Kenyan town called Modogashe. She highlighted that even though AI greatly supports her work, she remains the clinical officer. She explained that “AI is not perfect. It must not take over clinical work. But it can help us share across accessible healthcare. It can help discover what could have been missed early. We still need people to be trained, but AI tools can greatly support us.” Like Vyonne, Mamadou Ly also shared why and how AI can aid learning, especially in local languages. He said, “Education is not just about reading and writing. It is also an act of dignity.” Mamadou Ly at Goalkeepers Dakar 2026. item.title: LagosFashionWeek2026: Personal Style Is Alive and Well – Just Ask Ifeoma Odogwu
item.description: From runway shows to intimate presentations and the week’s most stylish gatherings, the fashion editor and creative consultant made a case for directional dressing with oodles of personality. Ifeoma Odogwu , better known as Hyperfashun , is easily one of the best dressed women in Lagos, and arguably on the continent and per usual her Lagos Fashion Week style is peerless. A familiar face in Nigeria’s fashion industry, the former Genevieve Magazine fashion editor, stylist to stars such as Toke Makinwa and more, the creative consultant has spent years working with designers, discovering emerging talent and helping shape the visual language of Nigerian fashion. So, naturally, when Lagos Fashion Week comes around, we’re just as interested in what she’s wearing as we are in what she’s watching. From the bustling Lagos Fashion Week tents at Federal Palace Hotel to a packed calendar of offsite presentations and fashion events across the city, Odogwu embraced the occasion with a wardrobe that made getting dressed part of the experience. At the tents, she joined the fashion crowd for presentations by Y’Wande , NYA The Label , E.S.O by Liman and FIA Factory , taking in some of the exciting design talent shaping the season. But as anyone familiar with Lagos Fashion Week knows, the shows have evolved. Some of the week’s most interesting moments happen elsewhere, and Odogwu’s itinerary reflected just how much the city’s fashion calendar has expanded. She made the rounds at presentations by Jewel Jemila , The Ladymaker, Rendoll, Kilentar, Onalaja and Orange Culture , and made time for the social side of fashion week, too, including the Made By Us pop-up at Melrose Loft and Tiffany Amber’s Breakfast Club. What makes Odogwu particularly interesting to watch is the perspective she brings to personal style. As someone whose career has been built around fashion imagery, designers and creative expression, her wardrobe offers another way of engaging with the industry she’s helped champion. Ifeoma has a certain clarity in her style and an unmatched point of view, something that’s often lacking in the sameness of our Instagram-driven world. Her style reminds us that what makes personal style compelling is individuality, curiosity and a willingness to have fun with fashion. Proudly supported by BellaNaija , The Girls’ Club proved that when women come together for movement, health, and community, magic happens. item.title: How the New Tax Stamp Could Show Up in Everyday Life
item.description: We’ve all been there: planning a weekend dinner with friends, throwing a birthday bash, or just kicking back at home with a few favourite treats. Drinks and refreshments are basically a staple of these moments. But have you ever stopped to think about how behind-the-scenes government policies end up changing the price tags on those items? With the Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) rolling out its new excise stamp policy in January 2026, that question is at the forefront, especially for brands that make things like alcohol, tobacco, and sugar-sweetened beverages. Honestly, nobody’s really stressing over the policy itself. What people care about is the ripple effect: how companies handle the new regulation and whether those adjustments will make our favourite items more expensive on the shelf. When Business Meets Your Wallet Behind every product is a mountain of decisions from packaging and distribution to compliance and production. Most of the time, we never see this happening, but it plays a huge role in how items are priced. When new regulations bring extra costs, companies find themselves at a crossroads. Some choose to absorb the blow internally to keep customers happy, while others might tweak their prices. It really comes down to the specific brand, the market, and how heavy the financial lift is. For everyday shoppers, that’s usually the moment a boring policy talk suddenly feels very real. What Does This Mean for How We Spend ? The change probably won’t hit overnight, and it might not even be dramatic. But over time, small shifts in everyday prices can change how we shop. You might find yourself comparing brands a bit more closely, hunting for promos and discounts, or rethinking how much cash you drop on certain treats. Brands, meanwhile, are caught in a tricky balancing act: keeping loyal customers without going broke on rising operating costs. Just keep in mind: a new tax stamp doesn’t automatically mean prices are shooting up. It all depends on how companies adapt and whether those extra costs trickle down to us. The Bigger Picture At the end of the day, this is really about finding a middle ground. The government wants solid systems to collect taxes, while businesses need a framework that lets them stay afloat and grow. But come to think of it, the authorities are already equipped with internal tracking solutions, such as electronic invoicing from FIRS alongside the Customs Service’s B’Odogwu digital excise register, rendering physical paper tags largely redundant. Striking that balance matters because business decisions don’t just stay on a spreadsheet. They shape the things we buy, the choices we make, and how we manage our money. Right now, it’s still a bit early to tell what the full impact on consumers will be. But staying clued in on what’s driving the market makes it a whole lot easier to navigate the changes coming our way. item.title: Who Checks on the Person Everyone Calls?
item.description: At 11:47 p.m., the family WhatsApp group suddenly comes alive. “Good evening, fam. Please, we have an emergency.” Before the second message arrives, everyone already knows who will be tagged. The eldest daughter who always knows what to do. The brother with the most stable job. The aunty abroad. The uncle in Lagos who “knows somebody.” The cousin with a car. The friend who always picks up, even at an unreasonable hour. In many Nigerian families, care has a name and a phone number. It belongs to the person who pays the unexpected bill, makes the difficult call, accompanies someone to the hospital, settles the family disagreement, or says, “Don’t worry, I’ll handle it.” We call them strong. Responsible. Dependable. We praise their shoulders without asking if they hurt. This is the human question at the heart of AXA Mansard’ s Culture of Care campaign: “ Who cares for the person everyone calls”? The Person Who Always Finds a Way Every family, friendship circle and workplace has one. Sometimes, she is the firstborn daughter who became a second mother long before she was ready. She remembers birthdays, school fees, hospital appointments, and the details everyone else forgets. Sometimes, he is the brother whose first good job quietly turned him into the family’s emergency fund and dependable source. His salary has not grown significantly, but the number of people depending on it has. Other times, it is the mom who serves everyone’s food before sitting down to eat. The father who never admits that he is worried. The friend who listens to everyone’s problems but rarely talks about her own. The colleague who carries the team whenever someone falls behind. These people are often so good at caring that we stop seeing the effort involved. We see the transfer alert, but not the personal plan they postponed. We see the paid bills, but not the hours spent calling doctors, arranging transport, and sitting beside a bed. We see the calm voice saying, “Everything will be fine,” but not the fear or uncertainty behind it. That person everyone calls may also be tired. They may worry about money, struggle with their health, or quietly wonder who would come through for them if they could no longer carry everyone else. Care Has More Than One Currency In Nigeria, many conversations about family responsibility often begin and end with money. Who paid the school fees? Who sent money home? Who handled the rent? Who covered the medical emergency? These questions matter, especially as the cost of living continues to stretch households. But money is only one currency of care. Care can also be time ! The sitting in traffic to pick up someone else’s child; the night spent at the hospital bedside; the regular reminder to an elderly parent to remember their medication. Or listening to the same worry repeatedly because the person telling you has nowhere else to take it. Care can be access ! Advice. Attention. Prayer. Food. Transport. Encouragement. A job referral. A place to stay. A

item.title: Meet Mo Odukoya: Pastor Jimmy Introduces His Wife to The Fountain of Life Church
item.description: Pastor Jimmy Odukoya and Pastor Mo Odukoya pose together following their formal church introduction If you’re a member of The Fountain of Life Church and you were at yesterday’s service, we’re a little jealous. What do you mean you got to witness Pastor Jimmy Odukoya introduce his wife, Mo Jasmine Daniel , to the congregation in person? Yes, right there at the church’s headquarters in Ilupeju, Lagos, the senior pastor had a special person to introduce, and he made sure everyone knew exactly who she was. As she joined him at the altar, he introduced her as Pastor Mo Odukoya , the church’s new first lady, and the congregation welcomed the couple with cheers and applause. Pastor Jimmy Odukoya and his wife, Mo Jasmine Daniel, holding hands during their official introduction at The Fountain of Life Church But before that introduction, Pastor Jimmy had a little story to tell. He spoke about how he had been navigating life alone since becoming the church’s senior pastor, and how he had been searching for someone to share the journey with. He invited Mo to join him, and the two walked up to the altar together, marking the moment with a warm reception from the congregation. Pastor Jimmy Odukoya introduces his wife, Mo Jasmine Daniel, on stage at The Fountain of Life Church in Ilupeju, Lagos For those who know Pastor Jimmy beyond the pulpit, there’s quite a bit to his story. He took over as senior pastor of The Fountain of Life Church in 2023, following the passing of his father, the late Pastor Taiwo Odukoya , who co-founded the ministry with his wife, Pastor Bimbo Odukoya . He is also an actor and musician, and film audiences may recognise him as Oba Ade in the 2022 historical film The Woman King, where he starred alongside Viola Davis . Pastor Jimmy Odukoya and Mo Jasmine Daniel after announcing their marriage to the congregation And now, there’s a new chapter to this story with Mo. Introduced to the congregation as Pastor Mo Odukoya, she is the daughter of Reverend Theophilus and Bolaji Daniel . She also took a moment to address the church, expressing her pleasure and honour at joining the ministry family. The couple also made sure their outfits were in sync for the occasion. Pastor Jimmy wore a structured burnt-orange native outfit with dark detailing on the cuffs and a matching necklace, while Pastor Mo chose a long-sleeved, floor-length dress in orange and copper patterns, finished with a matching clutch and accessories. Pastor Jimmy Odukoya and his new wife, Mo Jasmine Daniel, following their church introduction at The Fountain of Life Church *** Photo Credit: Pastor Jimmy Odukoya/Instagram The post Meet Mo Odukoya: Pastor Jimmy Introduces His Wife to The Fountain of Life Church appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: A New Map of ‘Empty’ Space Challenges a Tranquil Picture of the Galaxy
item.description: You might imagine space to be empty. But the seeming void contains a barely perceptible fog of hydrogen and other neutral atoms. In 2020, NASA’s New Horizons spacecraft, having passed the orbit of Pluto, measured a proxy for the amount of hydrogen around it. In the area between stars in our galaxy — the “interstellar medium,” or ISM — New Horizons found around 130 hydrogen atoms per liter of space. Source

item.title: Lunar Occultation of Venus
item.description: On Wednesday, June 17, skywatchers across the United States—and parts of Canada—enjoyed a rare event: a daytime lunar occultation of Venus. item.title: August Lunar Eclipse Rises Over Louisiana
item.description: A lunar eclipse is visible over southern Louisiana. The lunar eclipse was visible throughout much of North and South America and part of Europe and Africa between Aug. 27-28. The Full Moon slipped through Earth’s shadow on Aug. 27, continuing into Aug. 28 for some parts of the world, resulting in the lunar eclipse. At maximum eclipse, the Moon takes on a dramatic dark, ruddy or coppery tint along the covered edge. New Orleans is home to NASA’s Michoud Assembly Facility, where stages for NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket and structures for Orion spacecraft are produced for the Artemis missions.
